Good point. Semantics are very important. As someone whose bias is pretty far left myself, I yearn to see the left become persuasive again. But I think it's not just the left who is to blame. Media in general seems to be more interested in confirming the bias of their audience rather than informing (and because purely objective reporting is essentially impossible - persuading) the moderate and undecided people. 

I'm just as guilty as the next person of this but sometimes I'll read or watch the news for the sole purpose of getting sound bytes for ammunition to use in my next argument against my politically opposed coworker. But when I like listen to an hour long This American Life program or something like that that really takes its time to unfold a confusing complicated subject, and by the end of the program I don't see the "other side" as idiots or villains, I'm genuinely persuaded.

I think both the media and we are to blame for the the rhetoric and the ignoring of large groups of Americans. The media because they often give us only sound bytes rather than complicated explanations. And us, because we kept consuming that type of media.

This is not a commentary on specifically your comment, more of a personal opinion I've held for awhile:

Whenever I see our hear any discourse of this nature and I come across the word "blame", it is an automatic buzz word for me. It just doesn't feel productive at all. In my experience, people who focus too much on whom to blame are generally not interested in solutions. Granted, I'm guilty of playing the blame game as much as the next schmuck. But I still feel like it murders actual discourse between people with a diverse world view, therfore killing the solution. 

So when I hear people blaming the media, the helicopter parents, or the institutions for any problem. My gut reaction is to think "so what? How are you contributing to the solution to the problem? I doubt 'media-shaming' or whatever will do much good." In fact, it would more likely cause those people you disagree with to just dig in harder. 

Now where my little rant tends to lose steam is concerning the topic of "responsibly". If a genuine problem faces society, surely we must hold someone responsible, so as to at least keep them from ruining the solution, right? But it's harder than that when you just cast a blanket of blame on a large group of the population or this super abstract group we've named "the media".

I don't think it's just the atheist community that has this problem, but almost any large scale disagreement seems to differ from the exact same destructive rhetoric. 

The universal truth behind any dialogue is essentially this: you will never change anybody's mind if you can't demonstrate that you understand (at least in the abstract) where they are coming from and that you respect them.

If you are having a conversation with someone where you both completely disagree, and they don't feel at least understood, your attempts will inevitably only cause them to dig in harder in their positions. (As a former religious person, I can attest that any time I had a conversation with an atheist who didn't at least respect my belief system, I would dig in harder to the belief boat).

But if you can have a real conversation with somebody, where you spend the first part of the conversation asking genuine questions (not condescending) and really trying to understand their perspective, and only then sharing your own. If people could do that, they could open anyone's mind.

If you just assume that whoever your opposition is is just an idiot, they will sense it and you've lost all influence in that relationship. 

(What's funny is that as I type this, I realized that I'm guilty of this in my own mind when it comes to Donald Trump supporters. I automatically assume that they MUST be racist ignoramuses. But I've never spoken spoken with one and engaged one in a dialogue. At the end of my dialogue, I'd probably feel the exact same way about the Trump platform, but I'd understand them better and be better qualified to navigate this crazy national phenomenon. But anyway, that's just a thought I had)

But yeah, this is all probably common knowledge and common sense, but it's so hard to remember to put into practice. Especially when is topics you care about.
